Without full-removal calibration, the paired kernels matched the 99.9% knockdown observations yet predicted responses after complete removal that differed by 0.6 log-units, despite the imposed curvature bounds. The near-complete knockdowns and those bounds therefore did not make the removal response unique for this pair.
Does matching a 99.9% knockdown mean the kernels are almost certain to agree at complete removal?

No. A 99.9% knockdown leaves some of the species present; complete removal leaves none. In this example, agreement at the near-removal observation coexists with a 0.6 log-unit difference at the endpoint. Closeness in knockdown depth is not, by itself, agreement in the predicted response.
What does “without full-removal calibration” exclude?

It means observed full-removal responses were not used to calibrate the kernels for this analysis. The result asks what the available near-complete knockdown information and curvature bounds can establish without supplying an observed endpoint response as a calibration input.
Did the two kernels disagree on the 99.9% observations at all?

No. The reported result specifically says they matched the 99.9% knockdowns. Their disagreement concerns what they predict after complete removal, not a failure to match those near-complete observations.
What does the 0.6 log-unit number measure?

It measures the difference between the paired kernels’ predicted post-removal responses on the log-abundance scale. It is not a 0.6 log-unit error for either kernel against an observed outcome, and it is not a held-out log-RMSE.
Can we tell which kernel predicts the correct full-removal outcome?
Not from this evidence. It establishes that the compatible kernels predict different outcomes, but provides no observed full-removal outcome used to decide which prediction is correct.
Why didn't the curvature bounds force the two predictions to coincide?

The finding shows that the curvature restrictions used here still admitted both kernels and their different endpoint responses. A bound on how a response can bend need not fix its exact value at complete removal. The result does not give the mathematical bound or the kernels’ shapes, so we cannot assign a more specific mechanism for the remaining 0.6 log-unit difference.
Does this mean the curvature assumption was violated?

No. The difference remained *despite* the curvature bounds, which means those bounds did not eliminate the documented ambiguity. The evidence does not say that either kernel violated the assumed restriction.
Would a removal-response interval that includes both kernel predictions have to be at least 0.6 log-units wide?

For the same scalar post-removal log-abundance response, yes: an interval containing two values separated by 0.6 log-units must have width of at least 0.6 log-units. That is a consequence of the pair’s separation, not a reported width for a derived interval over every admissible kernel.
So has an exact 0.6 log-unit bound on the removal response been established?

No. The result gives a difference between two compatible kernel predictions. Other admissible responses, if any, could affect the full range, and no interval endpoints or exact response-bound width are reported.
What does this show about observational indistinguishability?

The near-complete knockdown observations do not distinguish these kernels, even with the stated curvature restrictions. Yet their full-removal predictions differ. For this pair and this observation set, agreement on what was observed does not imply agreement on the removal response.
Is the response therefore impossible to identify from any partial-knockdown design?

That would go beyond the example. It demonstrates remaining ambiguity for the documented kernels without full-removal calibration, despite matching 99.9% knockdowns and satisfying curvature bounds. It does not rule out identification under different observations or additional assumptions.
Could stronger curvature restrictions make the endpoint predictions agree?

That is not determined by this result. Stronger restrictions might exclude some response shapes, but one would need to state and justify them and then check what responses remain compatible. The evidence only establishes that the curvature bounds applied here did not remove the 0.6 log-unit divergence.
Does the difference tell us that a particular environmental forcing shift caused the aliasing?

No. The finding does not attribute the difference to a particular forcing shift or block. It states the observational match at 99.9% knockdown and the remaining post-removal disagreement under curvature bounds, without identifying an environmental cause.
Could we turn the 0.6 log-unit gap into a percentage improvement or deficit relative to gLV?

No. It is a difference between two post-removal predictions, not a comparison of prediction errors with generalized Lotka–Volterra. There is no matched gLV error or observed-outcome error in this result from which to calculate a performance percentage.
Would one of these kernels necessarily have a large error if an observed removal outcome became available?

The predictions are 0.6 log-units apart, so a single observed value cannot be equally close to both if it lies at one prediction. But the evidence does not supply that value or either kernel’s error. The important reported fact is their incompatible endpoint predictions, not a measured accuracy judgment.
Is the lesson that any prediction based on 99.9% knockdowns is unreliable?

No. A point prediction might perform well on a particular outcome. What this example shows is narrower: the stated observations and curvature bounds permit at least two different endpoint predictions, so a point prediction chosen from them is not uniquely determined by that information alone.
How should we describe the role of full-removal calibration without claiming it solves every identification problem?

Its absence defines the scope of this finding: the observed endpoint was not available to constrain the kernels. An observed removal response could add information about its case, but this result does not establish what any particular calibration scheme would identify for other removals. The reported ambiguity is specifically the one left without full-removal calibration.
Give me a careful statement of the evidence that keeps the match and divergence distinct.

In KnockdownAlias-8, without full-removal calibration, kernels matching the 99.9% knockdown observations still predicted complete-removal responses differing by 0.6 log-units despite curvature bounds. That documents residual endpoint ambiguity for the paired kernels; it does not report either kernel’s prediction error against an observed removal.
What is the decision about using knockdown kernels for species-removal predictions?

Use knockdown kernels only when selected full-removal outcomes are available for calibration. Otherwise, prefer dual-shock modeling. The reason for that condition is that uncalibrated kernels retain a 0.6-log-unit ambiguity in their predictions after complete removal.
What does “only with selected full-removal calibration” require?

It requires some selected complete-removal outcomes to be used as calibration information before relying on the knockdown kernels for removal predictions. Partial knockdowns alone do not satisfy that condition. The decision does not specify which removals are selected, how many there are, or a particular calibration procedure.
Does that mean we must observe the outcome of every removal we want to predict?

No. The decision says *selected* full removals, not every possible removal. It also does not guarantee that calibrating on a selected set uniquely determines responses for all other species or environmental conditions. The scope of what those observations constrain would still need to be made explicit.
Why isn't a 99.9% knockdown enough to count as full-removal calibration?

A 99.9% knockdown leaves some of the species present, while full removal leaves it absent. The decision rests on ambiguity that remains without an observed full-removal outcome: uncalibrated kernels can imply post-removal responses separated by 0.6 log-units. A near-complete knockdown should not be relabeled as an observation at complete removal.
What exactly is ambiguous by 0.6 log-units?

It is the difference between removal responses permitted by the uncalibrated kernels on the log-abundance scale. It is disagreement between possible predictions, not a measured 0.6-log-unit error against an observed outcome and not an RMSE.
Can we infer that each uncalibrated kernel would miss the true outcome by 0.6 log-units?

No. Their predictions differ from one another by 0.6 log-units; that does not locate the true outcome or give either kernel’s individual error. The decision uses the disagreement as a reason not to rely on a uniquely determined full-removal forecast from uncalibrated kernels.
Does the decision say that every uncalibrated kernel prediction has that same ambiguity?

No. The 0.6-log-unit ambiguity is the stated reason for this decision, not a claim that every removal or every possible community has exactly that degree of disagreement. Avoid turning the example into a universal numerical bound.
If a fitting algorithm picks one of the kernels, hasn't it resolved the ambiguity?

It has selected a forecast, but selection alone does not show that the observations determine that forecast. The stated ambiguity concerns differing full-removal responses that remain possible without full-removal calibration. The decision therefore conditions use of the knockdown kernels on selected endpoint observations rather than on a fitting algorithm returning one answer.
Does selected full-removal calibration prove the kernels will give identifiable predictions afterward?

The decision does not make that blanket claim. It sets a condition for using the kernels. What a selected removal calibrates, and whether any remaining compatible kernels agree on another removal response, would have to be assessed for the particular prediction.
Could we describe calibration as using a held-out removal outcome to correct its own prediction?

No. A selected outcome used for calibration is available information, whereas an outcome held out to evaluate a prediction must remain unavailable as its own answer. The decision requires selected full-removal calibration but does not authorize using a test case’s outcome to manufacture a prediction for that same case.
Why choose dual-shock modeling when full-removal calibration isn't available?

That is the fallback preference stated in the decision. Its explicit reason is the 0.6-log-unit removal-response ambiguity retained by uncalibrated knockdown kernels. The decision does not say dual-shock modeling is free from every identifiability limitation, or that it will outperform every alternative in every setting.
Is dual-shock modeling preferred even when the kernels have been calibrated using selected removals?

That is not the rule stated here. The choice permits knockdown kernels when selected full-removal calibration is available; *otherwise* it prefers dual-shock modeling. It does not impose a universal ranking between the two approaches in the calibrated setting.
What if we have only partial knockdowns and spike-in measurements, but no observed complete removals?

Then the condition for using knockdown kernels is not met. Under the decision, prefer dual-shock modeling rather than treating the partial knockdowns and spike-ins as though they supplied selected full-removal calibration. The reason remains the stated 0.6-log-unit ambiguity in uncalibrated removal responses.
Does the choice mean partial-knockdown observations are useless without complete-removal calibration?

No. The decision is about when to *use knockdown kernels for full-removal predictions*. It does not say partial-knockdown observations have no information or that no other question can be studied with them. It says they do not, in this decision, replace selected full-removal calibration for using those kernels.
Could a curvature assumption stand in for selected full-removal calibration?

Not under the decision as stated. It calls for selected full-removal calibration and gives the retained 0.6-log-unit ambiguity of uncalibrated kernels as its reason. One should not silently treat an assumption about near-removal behavior as though it were an observed complete-removal outcome.
Are we claiming that the 0.6-log-unit ambiguity disappears for all removals as soon as a selected removal is calibrated?

No. The decision does not quantify ambiguity after calibration or state that it disappears for every species. Selected full-removal outcomes are a condition for using the kernels; the reach of that calibration must not be extended beyond what is established for the responses of interest.
Does preferring dual-shock modeling tell us what its uncertainty intervals should be?

No. The decision names dual-shock modeling as the preferred approach when selected full-removal calibration is absent. It does not prescribe intervals, an uncertainty-calibration method, or an interval-coverage result for dual-shock predictions.
Should the reason for the choice be described as poor RMSE for uncalibrated kernels?

Not here. The reason explicitly stated is that uncalibrated kernels retain a 0.6-log-unit ambiguity after removal. That quantity is a difference between compatible removal predictions, not an RMSE comparison. Replacing it with an unsupported error claim would change the decision’s rationale.
Could I say dual-shock modeling resolves that particular 0.6-log-unit ambiguity?

The decision does not establish that. It prefers dual-shock modeling *instead of relying on uncalibrated knockdown kernels* in the absence of selected full-removal calibration. It does not say the two methods have the same admissible model class or that a dual-shock fit resolves every ambiguity present in the kernel construction.
How would you state the decision in one sentence while preserving its condition and reason?

Use knockdown kernels only with selected full-removal calibration; when that calibration is unavailable, prefer dual-shock modeling because uncalibrated kernels retain 0.6 log-units of ambiguity in their post-removal responses.
Could a consumer–resource model provide another way to study species-removal responses from compositional microbial time series?

The proposal is to fit mass-balanced consumer–resource dynamics to compositions, metabolomics, and sparse biomass anchors, then profile observationally equivalent models for their removal responses. It combines a dynamical account of species and resources with an explicit check on whether models that fit the available observations predict the same outcome after a species is removed. It is a proposal, not a completed fit or an identifiability result.
What does “consumer–resource dynamics” add to the description of the community?

It represents species in relation to resources they may consume or affect, rather than describing species abundances alone. A species-removal forecast would then concern how the modeled species and resources respond when that species is absent. The proposal does not specify particular species–resource relationships or equations.
And what does “mass-balanced” mean here?

It means the proposed dynamics must respect a stated accounting of material as it moves among the components represented in the model. That can constrain which dynamical descriptions are admissible. It does not mean every relevant resource is measured, that the system has no exchange with its environment, or that mass balance alone identifies a unique removal response; the accounting and its scope would have to be defined.
Would mass balance let us recover absolute species abundances directly from compositional observations?

Not directly. Compositions provide relative abundances, so their absolute scale remains a distinct issue. Sparse biomass anchors contribute information about scale at the points where they apply. Mass-balance constraints may restrict compatible dynamics, but they do not turn proportions into a continuously observed absolute-abundance trajectory by themselves.
What do the biomass anchors measure in this proposal?

They are sparse measurements anchoring biomass in the proposed fit. The description does not specify their measurement method, sampling interval, or whether they resolve the abundance of each species separately. Those details would matter to a formal identifiability analysis, but they are not part of the proposal as stated.
Should I carry over a particular anchor interval from another setup?

No interval is specified for these biomass anchors. The proposal should be described as using sparse biomass anchors without assigning them a sampling schedule or assuming they provide measurements between anchor times.
What does metabolomics contribute if we already observe compositions?

It adds observations about metabolites or resources that compositions alone do not provide. Those observations may constrain the consumer–resource dynamics and help distinguish candidate explanations of the species trajectories. Their presence does not guarantee that every resource is observed or that a measured metabolite change can be attributed uniquely to one species.
If a metabolite changes when a species changes, can we conclude that species consumed it?

Not from that association alone. Other species and environmental influences could contribute to the metabolite trajectory. The proposed model can express candidate consumer–resource relationships, but claiming a particular one is determined would require assumptions and observations that distinguish it from compatible alternatives.
Are metabolomics measurements the same thing as measuring all the resource flows?

No. Measuring metabolite states and identifying flows are different. The proposal includes metabolomics as an observational input, but does not specify its coverage or say it directly measures all uptake, production, or exchange. The mass-balance accounting would have to be interpreted in light of what is actually observed.
Why fit compositions, metabolomics, and biomass anchors together rather than treating them as three separate answers?

They constrain different aspects of a shared dynamical description. Compositions constrain relative species trajectories; metabolomics constrains the observed metabolite trajectories; sparse biomass anchors constrain some absolute-scale information. A model compatible with all three must account for their joint observations. Agreement with each input is still distinct from agreement on what would happen after removal.
Does adding metabolomics eliminate environmental confounding?

Not automatically. Environmental variation could influence species and measured metabolites alike. Metabolomics can provide relevant distinctions, but whether it separates environmental influences from consumer–resource interactions depends on the specified model, observation set, and assumptions. The proposal does not assert that confounding has been eliminated.
What should “observationally equivalent” mean for these models?

It should mean that the models cannot be distinguished using the observations made available for this analysis: the compositional time series, metabolomics, and sparse biomass anchors, under a clearly stated compatibility criterion. Models should not be called equivalent merely because they fit the compositions if an available metabolomics measurement or biomass anchor distinguishes them.
Do observationally equivalent models need identical resource-use relationships?

Not necessarily. Equivalence concerns what is observed, not equality of every internal relationship. Different consumer–resource descriptions may produce the same available species, metabolite, and biomass observations. The question is whether differences left unresolved by those observations matter to a removal prediction.
What does it mean to profile their removal responses?

Consider the removal response implied by each admissible model that matches the specified observations, rather than reporting only the response from one selected fit. The profile shows which responses remain possible within that compatible set. Its interpretation depends on defining both the admissible models and the particular removal response being compared.
Would the profile automatically produce a single removal prediction?

No. It could reveal agreement across compatible models, or it could reveal differing responses. A fitting procedure can select one model and output one forecast, but profiling asks whether the observations and assumptions warrant treating that forecast as uniquely determined.
Can you give a general illustration of how observational agreement and removal disagreement could coexist?

Two mass-balanced consumer–resource descriptions might reproduce the same observed species compositions, measured metabolite trajectories, and available biomass anchors while assigning the underlying resource dynamics differently. When a species is removed, those different assignments might lead to different modeled responses. That is a conceptual possibility to examine, not a reported example or a finding that it occurs in this proposed fit.
Would the metabolomics data necessarily distinguish those two descriptions?

Only if the measured metabolites and their variation reveal the relevant difference. Both candidate descriptions in the illustration were assumed to match the available metabolomics observations. Unobserved distinctions could still matter after removal, so whether metabolomics breaks a particular ambiguity must be checked, not assumed.
If two compatible models predict different metabolite trajectories after removal, does that imply their species responses also differ?

Not necessarily. Their modeled metabolite responses could differ without changing the particular species log-abundance response of interest, or a difference in resource dynamics could affect it. Profiling should keep the response being assessed explicit instead of treating all internal differences as equivalent to different species-removal predictions.
Conversely, could their predicted species responses differ even when they match every measured metabolite before removal?

Yes, that is the sort of ambiguity the proposal is meant to examine. Matching metabolite measurements before an intervention does not by itself force agreement about how the community adjusts to removing a species. A conclusion either way requires the stated model assumptions and a comparison across all compatible descriptions.
Does profiling identify which individual consumer–resource parameters are uniquely known?

Not just by producing a removal-response profile. Parameter identifiability and response identifiability are distinct. Some internal parameters might remain uncertain even if all compatible models agree on a particular removal response; alternatively, unresolved parameters might lead to divergent responses. The proposal specifically calls for profiling removal responses.
What assumptions would be needed to call a profiled removal response identifiable?

The model class, mass-balance accounting, observation process, and scope of the removal intervention would need to be stated. A sufficient response-level condition would then require every admissible model compatible with the compositions, metabolomics, and sparse biomass anchors to imply the same specified removal response. The proposal does not yet supply those sufficient conditions.
If the profile contains several responses, could it still be useful?

Yes. It can characterize what remains unresolved instead of disguising it as one definite forecast. For a specified response, its range across compatible models can describe model-conditional ambiguity, provided the compatible set and response are defined. No numerical range or interval width is stated in this proposal.
Would such a range be a confidence interval?

Not automatically. A range obtained by profiling observationally equivalent models describes responses compatible with a defined model class and observation criterion. A confidence interval would require an additional statistical coverage interpretation that the proposal does not provide.
When profiling responses, should the removal outcome itself be used to decide which models are observationally equivalent?

If the purpose is to ask what the pre-removal observations imply about a removal, the outcome being predicted should not be supplied as its own answer in the equivalence criterion. The profile should say explicitly which compositions, metabolomics measurements, and biomass anchors are available for fitting and which removal response is being forecast.
Does this proposal imply we have already benchmarked the resulting forecasts against generalized Lotka–Volterra?

No. It describes a model-fitting and observational-equivalence approach, with no reported held-out removal error or baseline comparison. Understanding what the observations identify and measuring how well a forecast predicts held-out responses are separate questions.
Is mass balance the key guarantee that profiles will collapse to one answer?

It is a constraint on admissible dynamics, not an automatic guarantee of a unique removal answer. Different mass-balanced models could still fit the available compositions, metabolomics, and sparse biomass anchors. The profile is needed precisely to determine whether their removal responses coincide or diverge under the assumptions eventually specified.
What is the careful formulation of the proposal without making an identifiability claim too early?

Fit mass-balanced consumer–resource dynamics jointly to compositional observations, metabolomics, and sparse biomass anchors, then profile the removal responses of observationally equivalent models. The profile would show whether those observations and the stated model assumptions determine a particular species-removal response or leave multiple responses possible; neither outcome is asserted in advance.
Given the limits of calibrating knockdown-based forecasts, what should we test in the consumer–resource approach?

The plan is to test measured resource pulses for three things: whether they provide flux-rank identifiability, what bounds remain on removal responses across observationally equivalent models, and how accurately the resulting knockout predictions perform in log-abundance RMSE against generalized Lotka–Volterra (gLV) models using matched observations. These are planned tests, not established findings.
What makes a resource pulse useful for an identifiability test?

A resource pulse could introduce measured variation that helps distinguish resource flows within mass-balanced consumer–resource dynamics. The question is whether that variation reveals directions that were otherwise indistinguishable. A change in a measured resource does not, by itself, prove that the relevant flows or removal responses are identified.
Why emphasize that the pulses are measured?

The plan calls for measured resource pulses so that the resource variation is part of the information available to the analysis. Its observed values can then be related to the compositional, metabolomics, and biomass observations in a stated model. The plan does not specify how pulses are measured or claim that measuring them directly reveals every resource flux.
Are these pulses species knockdowns?

No. A resource pulse changes a resource-related input; a knockdown reduces a species. Here the pulses are proposed to probe consumer–resource dynamics, while the prediction being evaluated concerns a species knockout. Observing one kind of perturbation does not automatically reveal the response to the other.
Does the plan say which resources are pulsed or when?

No. It does not name a resource, pulse magnitude, count, or schedule. Those design details would have to be specified for the test; they should not be inferred from the phrase “measured resource pulses.”
What exactly is flux-rank identifiability?

It concerns whether the variation available to the consumer–resource analysis distinguishes the resource-flux directions relevant to its claims. A formal test must define the flux representation, the rank being checked, and which effects that rank is intended to identify. The plan asks for this analysis; it does not state a rank value or assert that the measured pulses achieve full rank.
If measured metabolites change after a pulse, does that establish flux rank?

No. A change shows a response, but different underlying flows could still produce compatible measured metabolite trajectories. Flux-rank identifiability asks whether the observations distinguish those flows in the specified model, not merely whether a pulse has a visible effect.
Does mass balance guarantee that the fluxes are distinguishable?

Mass balance constrains admissible dynamics, but it does not alone guarantee that available observations distinguish every compatible flux arrangement. The proposed flux-rank test needs to consider the constraints together with measured pulse variation and the observation process.
Should I assume all resource fluxes have to be identified before we can predict a knockout?

Not necessarily. Identification of every internal flux is stronger than identification of a particular removal response. The analysis should say which flux distinctions matter to the knockout prediction. It should also check whether descriptions that remain indistinguishable in flux terms nevertheless agree—or disagree—on the removal response.
Is that why the plan includes removal-equivalence bounds as a separate test?

Yes. Flux-rank analysis examines distinguishability in the resource dynamics; removal-equivalence bounds examine what species-removal responses remain possible across models compatible with the available observations and assumptions. One should not treat a rank finding, whatever it turns out to be, as an automatic numerical bound on a knockout response.
What does removal equivalence mean in this setting?

It asks whether observationally equivalent consumer–resource descriptions imply the same specified outcome after a species is removed. If they imply different outcomes, bounds can express the range of responses they permit. The model class, observation set, and removal response must be defined before a bound can be interpreted.
Which observations should those descriptions have to match?

The compatibility criterion should include the observations used in the analysis: species compositions, metabolomics, sparse biomass anchors, and the measured resource-pulse information where it is available. Calling two models equivalent after checking only compositions would overlook measurements that could distinguish them. The plan does not supply a formal equivalence criterion.
Would the knockout outcome itself be used to narrow those equivalence classes?

Not if the purpose is to bound what the available observations imply about that held-out knockout. Supplying an outcome as its own answer would obscure the prediction question. The analysis should state which observations define compatibility and which post-knockout outcomes are reserved for evaluating forecasts.
Can the bounds be narrow even if some fluxes remain ambiguous?

In principle, yes: different compatible flux descriptions could yield the same or similar response to a particular removal. The opposite is also possible. Deriving removal-equivalence bounds checks the response directly rather than assuming its ambiguity has the same extent as ambiguity in the underlying fluxes.
Do we know how wide the removal-equivalence bounds will be?
No. The plan is to determine them. It provides no endpoints, widths, species-specific results, or guarantee that the bounds will collapse to a single response.
Are those bounds confidence intervals?

Not merely by being bounds. A removal-equivalence bound describes responses permitted by an explicitly defined observationally compatible model class. A confidence interval would make an additional statistical coverage claim, which is not specified in this plan.
What does the knockout log-RMSE test add if we already derive bounds?

It evaluates predictive accuracy against held-out knockout abundances on the logarithmic scale. Bounds address what the observations and assumptions leave possible; log-RMSE measures how closely point forecasts match evaluated outcomes. The plan includes both because a narrow bound does not itself report held-out accuracy, and a low error would not itself prove identifiability.
Why compare that RMSE with gLV?

The matched gLV model supplies the specified baseline for the knockout prediction comparison. The methods should have access to the same observations, so an error difference is not attributed to one approach receiving extra compositional, metabolomics, biomass, or measured-pulse information. Matching observations does not require matching model structures.
Is a 20% reduction already part of this plan’s result?

No result is reported. The broader prediction objective is a 20% reduction in held-out post-removal log-abundance RMSE versus gLV models using identical observations. This plan calls for a matched knockout log-RMSE benchmark, but gives neither method’s RMSE nor a percentage improvement.
Could the resource pulses make the consumer–resource model appear better just because gLV does not receive them?

That would not be an observation-matched comparison. The benchmark should give both approaches access to the same available observations, including measured pulse information when it is part of the prediction inputs. They may use that information differently, but unequal access would answer a different question.
Does a favorable gLV comparison show that the flux-rank condition held?

No. A lower held-out knockout log-RMSE would be a performance finding. Flux-rank identifiability needs its own analysis of the combined dynamics and measured variation. Likewise, a rank finding would not supply an RMSE comparison without testing predictions.
What should we conclude if observationally equivalent models still predict different knockouts?

The removal-equivalence analysis would have to reflect that disagreement in its bounds for the specified response. A point forecast could still be evaluated for accuracy, but it should not be described as uniquely determined by those observations and assumptions. This is a possible outcome of the planned analysis, not a finding reported here.
Does the plan assume that environmental variation is fully controlled by the measured resource pulses?

No. Environmental confounding remains something the model and identifiability argument must address. Measured resource pulses can supply relevant variation, but the plan does not state that they capture every environmental influence or guarantee separation of environmental forcing from consumer–resource effects.
How should the tests fit together without making one stand in for another?

First define what resource flows and observations the mass-balanced consumer–resource analysis considers, then test whether measured resource pulses provide the required flux-rank distinctions. Derive removal-equivalence bounds for models compatible with those observations, and separately measure held-out knockout log-abundance RMSE against observation-matched gLV. The plan states these aims without specifying an outcome or requiring that one test’s result imply another’s.
Can you state the plan succinctly, including why we are pursuing it?

Given knockdown calibration limits, test whether measured resource pulses distinguish the fluxes relevant to removal prediction, bound the removal responses still possible across observationally equivalent consumer–resource models, and compare held-out knockout log-abundance RMSE with gLV using matched observations. Whether the pulses identify the needed effects, narrow the bounds, or improve prediction remains to be determined.
How would we use measured resource pulses to examine both SentinelBounds v1 and KnockdownAlias-8?

Extend the observational-equivalence profiles in SentinelBounds v1 and the paired-kernel aliases in KnockdownAlias-8 with measured resource-pulse information. Then evaluate mass-balanced flux rank and knockout log-abundance RMSE. This is an activity to perform; it does not report a rank, an error value, or whether the additional observations distinguish any models.
What does it mean to extend an observational-equivalence profile with pulses?

It means reassessing which model descriptions remain compatible when the measured resource-pulse observations are included alongside the observations defining the profile. Models that agreed before the added information might or might not remain indistinguishable afterward. The activity does not state the result of that reassessment.
And how does the same idea apply to the KnockdownAlias-8 kernels?

Assess the paired kernels against the added resource-pulse observations. The question is whether they still agree on what is observed or whether the pulses distinguish them. That test is separate from asking whether either kernel accurately predicts a knockout.
Do we need to assume that the two artifacts contain the same kind of model?

No. The activity uses profiles from SentinelBounds v1 and aliases from KnockdownAlias-8 as two subjects for the resource-pulse extension. It does not say their models have identical structures or that their compatibility criteria are interchangeable. Each comparison needs its own clearly stated observation set and model assumptions.
Why specify measured resource pulses rather than resource pulses alone?

The measurements provide information about the resource perturbations that can be included in the observational comparison and the flux-rank analysis. Knowing that a pulse occurred without defining what was measured would leave unclear which distinctions the analysis can actually make. Measurement does not, by itself, establish that the underlying fluxes are identifiable.
Are the resource pulses complete species removals?

No. Resource pulses perturb the resource side of the proposed analysis. Knockout log-RMSE concerns predictions of outcomes after species removal. A measured response to a resource pulse can inform a model, but it should not be treated as an observed knockout outcome.
What does “mass-balanced flux rank” ask us to evaluate?

It asks whether the measured variation distinguishes the flux directions relevant to a mass-balanced consumer–resource description. The evaluation needs to define the flux representation, how mass balance constrains it, and the matrix or other object whose rank is measured. This activity names the rank assessment but supplies no rank figure or sufficiency condition.
If the metabolite trajectories visibly respond to a resource pulse, does that prove the needed flux rank?

No. Visible change shows that an observed quantity responded; distinct underlying flux descriptions might still explain that change. Rank concerns whether the relevant flux contributions are distinguishable within the specified mass-balanced analysis. It must be checked rather than inferred from a changing trajectory.
Could mass balance alone make two otherwise indistinguishable models separable?

Mass balance limits which descriptions are admissible, but its effect depends on the stated accounting and the available observations. The activity is to assess flux rank with measured resource pulses, not to presume that mass balance alone—or the pulses alone—resolves every ambiguity.
Should the rank analysis include every possible resource flow?

The scope has to be defined. The phrase “mass-balanced flux rank” does not specify an exhaustive inventory of resource flows or claim they are all observed. A reported rank would need to identify which modeled flux directions it concerns and which measurements support the calculation.
If the flux rank turns out to be full, would that prove a unique knockout response?

Not automatically. Full rank of a defined flux design could help distinguish flux contributions, but removal-response identification would require showing that all admissible models matching the observations agree on the particular knockout response. Rank and intervention-level agreement are related questions, not interchangeable conclusions.
Conversely, could a flux-rank deficiency coexist with accurate knockout predictions?

In principle, yes. Ambiguity in an internal flux direction need not change every removal response, and a predictor could also have low error on evaluated knockouts without being uniquely determined by the observations. Measuring both flux rank and knockout log-RMSE keeps those issues separate.
What should count as an observation when we test whether profiles or aliases remain equivalent?

Use an explicitly defined observation set for each analysis and include the measured resource-pulse information being added. The existing observations used by each profile or alias comparison should not be silently discarded. Equivalence means agreement on the information actually made available for that comparison, not merely agreement on one convenient trajectory.

In ResourceAlias-8 v2, complete pool labeling achieved augmented flux rank 14/14 and 92% removal-bound coverage, with knockout log-RMSE of 0.24 versus 0.32 for observation-matched gLV—a 25% reduction—while labeling omissions retained aliasing.
What is the decision about using consumer–resource models for species-removal forecasts?

Retain consumer–resource forecasts only with comprehensive ¹³C pool tracing. The reason is that untraced cross-feeding can defeat apparently full-rank flux fits: a full-rank calculation for the assessed fluxes need not settle removal responses when relevant cross-fed pools remain untraced.
What does “only with” mean here?

It makes comprehensive ¹³C pool tracing a condition for retaining these consumer–resource forecasts. If that tracing is unavailable, an apparently full-rank flux fit is not enough to justify retaining them under this decision.
Does comprehensive tracing mean every metabolite that could possibly exist must be labeled?

The decision does not define a universal inventory of metabolites or a labeling protocol. “Comprehensive” must be understood relative to the cross-fed pools relevant to the consumer–resource forecast and its removal-response claim. It should not be reduced to tracing only convenient pools while leaving a removal-relevant cross-feeding route unexamined.
Why isn't a full-rank flux fit sufficient on its own?

A rank statement applies to the flux design that was actually assessed. Cross-feeding through an untraced pool can matter to a removal response without being distinguished by that design. The decision explicitly treats that gap between apparent flux rank and removal-relevant information as the reason to require comprehensive tracing.
Are we saying the rank calculation is incorrect whenever cross-feeding is untraced?

No. It may correctly report full rank for its defined directions. The problem is extending that statement beyond its scope, as though it also distinguished contributions from untraced cross-fed pools. “Apparently full-rank” cautions against that inference; it does not assert an arithmetic error in the rank calculation.
Does a model cease to be mass-balanced if it omits a traced pool?

That conclusion is not part of the decision. Mass balance and observational completeness are different questions. A fit can satisfy its stated accounting while an untraced cross-feeding contribution still undermines what the fit establishes about species-removal responses.
What is it about removal that makes an untraced pool consequential?

The forecast concerns how the community responds when a species is absent, not just whether a model fits observations with that species present. If compatible descriptions leave a cross-feeding contribution unresolved, they need not imply the same removal response. The decision does not specify a particular metabolite, species, or pathway; it sets a condition intended to address that kind of ambiguity.
Does requiring tracing mean the removal response is automatically identifiable?

No. Comprehensive ¹³C pool tracing is a condition for retaining the forecasts, not a stand-alone theorem of identifiability. A response-level claim would still need a defined observation set, model assumptions, and an argument that observationally compatible descriptions agree on the specified removal response.
Could a traced model still have uncertain removal responses?

The decision does not rule that out. Tracing supplies information about cross-feeding, but its presence alone does not say that every compatible model gives an identical removal trajectory. The scope of any remaining uncertainty must be assessed for the response being forecast.
Why specify ¹³C pool tracing rather than just more metabolomics observations?

The decision specifically requires comprehensive ¹³C pool tracing. It does not claim that an unspecified increase in metabolomics measurements provides equivalent information about cross-feeding. Nor does it prescribe which substrate to label or when to sample the resulting traces.
Would time-resolved measurements be part of what we mean by comprehensive tracing?

The decision names comprehensive ¹³C pool tracing but gives no temporal sampling rule. Whatever observations are used must be sufficient to address the removal-relevant cross-feeding left unresolved by an apparently full-rank fit; a particular number of time points or sampling interval is not stated here.
If we obtain a strong ¹³C signal from one pool, have we met the condition?

Signal strength from one pool does not by itself establish comprehensive coverage of the cross-feeding relevant to the forecast. The issue is whether consequential pools remain untraced, not merely whether a tracer signal can be detected. The decision provides no numerical signal threshold.
Are we adopting consumer–resource forecasts whenever that tracing is present, regardless of prediction quality?

The decision sets a condition for retaining the forecasts; it does not guarantee their accuracy or waive evaluation of removal predictions. Likewise, it provides no new log-abundance RMSE, interval coverage, or benchmark result. Tracing addresses the stated concern about untraced cross-feeding, while predictive performance remains a distinct question.
Does this decision say that all consumer–resource models without ¹³C measurements are wrong?

No. It concerns whether to retain their species-removal forecasts under the stated cross-feeding concern. It is not a claim that every fit without tracing is numerically wrong, that all its other uses fail, or that every removal in every community depends on an untraced pool.
Could I express the condition as “use the forecast if the observed flux matrix is full rank”?

That would omit the decisive condition. The decision requires comprehensive ¹³C pool tracing precisely because apparently full-rank flux fits can be defeated by untraced cross-feeding. Rank of a narrower observed matrix cannot substitute for tracing the relevant pools.
What if we trace many pools but cannot establish that the coverage is comprehensive?

Then the stated condition has not been established merely by counting labeled pools. A claim that tracing is comprehensive needs to identify its scope relative to the cross-feeding relevant to the forecast. The decision does not provide a pool count that would settle that assessment.
Does “retain” imply combining consumer–resource forecasts with another prediction method?

No combination rule is stated. The choice concerns retaining consumer–resource forecasts only under the comprehensive-tracing condition. It does not name a replacement method for cases without that tracing or specify how to combine forecasts.
Would full augmented flux rank be sufficient evidence that no cross-fed pool was omitted?

Not without knowing what the augmented design includes. Full rank within a specified design says its represented directions are distinguishable; it does not, on its own, certify that no removal-relevant pool lies outside it. The tracing requirement keeps that distinction explicit.
Can I describe the reason as an observed percentage of missed removals?

The decision gives no percentage, error value, or number of missed removals. Its explicit reason is qualitative: untraced cross-feeding defeats apparently full-rank flux fits. Adding a numerical rationale here would go beyond the decision.
What is a careful one-sentence statement of the choice?

Retain consumer–resource species-removal forecasts only with comprehensive ¹³C pool tracing, because untraced cross-feeding can defeat the removal-response conclusions suggested by apparently full-rank flux fits.
